bib.title: Your data science could use some engineering (Chapter 2, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: How should data science work be framed and run (simplicity, Agile, MLOps) so ML projects succeed and stay maintainable?
contributions: Defines ML engineering as technology, people and process

results.claim: Simplicity is the foundation of ML engineering and informs scoping and implementation.
results.setup: Chapter 2 of a practitioner book; author's experience, not a controlled study
results.quote: It is by far the single most important aspect of ML engineering, as it will inform all other aspects of project work, scoping, and implementation details.

results.claim: Collaboration between the ML team and the business unit is the biggest driver of success with least rework; communication within the ML team is second.
results.setup: Chapter 2 of a practitioner book; author's experience, not a controlled study
results.quote: The single biggest driving factor in making a successful project that has the least amount of rework is collaborative involvement between the ML team and the business unit.

results.claim: Anecdote: a team of 12 data scientists spent 10 months productionising a GAN for image upscaling, then the team was let go within 12 weeks of consultants arriving and the project abandoned.
results.setup: One unnamed company, told as an anecdote by the author; no identification or verification
results.quote: One of the more notable ones was a GAN for image-resolution upscaling

results.claim: Plan for change: goals at project start never matched what was built; loosely coupled modular design limits the cost of pivots.
results.setup: Chapter 2 of a practitioner book; author's experience, not a controlled study
results.quote: In nearly every ML project I've worked on, the goals defined at the beginning of the project never turned out to be exactly what was built by the end.

results.claim: ML needs extra internal demos beyond software peer review: show performance as a function of input data, functionality and output visualisations.
results.setup: Chapter 2 of a practitioner book; author's experience, not a controlled study
results.quote: For ML work, it's important to show the performance as a function of how it affects the data being passed into your code, demonstrate functionality, and show visualizations of the output.

results.claim: MLOps = DevOps plus parameter/metrics tracking, model registration, A/B testing and bandits, prediction-accuracy and retraining monitoring.
results.setup: Chapter 2 of a practitioner book; author's experience, not a controlled study
results.quote: Just as DevOps augments software engineering work, MLOps augments ML engineering work.

limits: No data or experiments; all claims are the author's experience.
Failure-rate claims dismissed as vendor marketing without evidence.
Authors and year not printed in the excerpted chapter PDF.
practices: Pursue the simplest solution that solves the problem; walk the ladder from quick wins (visualisation, aggregation, single equation) to heuristics, classic ML, then deep learning/AI only if needed (Fig 2.2, sec 2.2).
Monitor a simple implementation and move up in complexity only if value is no longer realised (Fig 2.2).
Demo to team members and customers during development rather than building a full solution in isolation (Figs 2.4, 2.5, sec 2.3.1).
Even a one-person team should seek peer review and SME demos (p.34).
Assume nothing about the data; always validate and analyze (Fig 2.3).
Design modular, loosely coupled code so requirement changes do not force full rewrites (sec 2.3.2).
Evaluate ML work with quantitative and qualitative measures and agreed success criteria (Figs 2.1, 2.3).
Adopt MLOps additions over DevOps: versioning plus registration, A/B testing with statistical evaluation, bandits, parameter and metrics tracking, retraining and fallback-rate monitoring (Fig 2.7).

terms.definition: brings the core functional capabilities of a data scientist, a data engineer, and a software engineer into a hybrid role
the application of similar principles that DevOps has to software development, adapted to ML (Fig 2.7)
